strengths: The paper addresses a useful question for vision-language data collection: whether captions originally written in different languages provide complementary visual information. Its contribution is an empirical analysis with practical implications for multilingual training and annotation.

The comparisons use the same images and are designed to match caption-set sizes, helping distinguish multilingual variation from simply collecting more captions. Coverage gains appear in Crossmodal human captions and two model sources. Visual Genome grounding provides stronger evidence than graph size alone: Vertex object coverage increases from 9.6% for English to 11.5% for multilingual sets (Table 3).

The supplementary human study provides additional supporting evidence: 20 English/Japanese speakers captioning 30 images yield multilingual increases of 8.4% in objects, 7.7% in relations, and 6.5% in attributes. The translation audit with 15 native speakers also supports substantial preservation of semantic content.

Fine-tuning on English translations controls the output language and generally reveals differences associated with the captions' source language. This supports the narrower conclusion that these caption distributions contain learnable differences.
weaknesses: Central numerical results contain unresolved inconsistencies. Table 14, attributed to LLaVA captions, exactly reproduces all 36 corresponding entries of the Vertex results in Table 4, including multilingual training and evaluation. This prevents treating it as convincing independent replication. Table 2 reports a Vertex attribute average of 1.98 although its language-specific values average approximately 1.69. Table 15 also contradicts the universal same-language-best claim: Chinese training scores 0.124 on Chinese references, versus 0.131 for multilingual training. These issues affect quantitative conclusions, beyond presentation polish.

Semantic measurement validity is only partially established. Results depend on FLAN-T5 parsing and WordNet/embedding-based concept merging, without a reported parser audit or sensitivity analysis of merging choices. Additional graph entries can reflect synonym fragmentation or hallucinations. Visual Genome object recall is a valuable check, but it does not validate precision or the substantial claimed gains in relations and attributes.

The expressive-variation claims have weaker validation than the semantic claims. The human translation audit assesses content preservation in model-generated captions; it does not establish preservation of tone, authenticity, or other LIWC dimensions in human captions. Applying English LIWC after GPT-4 translation can conflate original expression with translation choices. Near-chance source-language classification and multilingual embedding results do not eliminate this concern.

Some interpretations exceed what the comparisons identify. Section 3.2 cannot rule out language-conditioned generation modes merely because within-model multilingual variation resembles variation across different English-captioning models. Likewise, language-associated caption differences do not isolate perceptual preferences from verbosity, annotator population, or descriptive conventions. The fine-tuning results establish adaptation to reference distributions, while improved visual understanding remains a hypothesis.

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting are incomplete. Exact LLaVA/GIT checkpoints, decoding settings, caption-selection procedures, and GIT training hyperparameters are insufficiently specified. Main coverage and fine-tuning tables lack uncertainty estimates, although selected supplementary analyses report significance. Overall, the recurring coverage gains and human evidence support a worthwhile descriptive contribution, but measurement uncertainty and inconsistencies in central results keep the recommendation near the acceptance boundary.
